opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most important shifts for us. Up until now, most of how these robot foundation models got better was through imitation: you collect demonstrations, usually teleoperated by people, and the model learns to copy what it sees. That gets you remarkably far. You get a policy that can fold laundry or make a coffee in a way that looks pretty competent. But imitation has a ceiling. The model can only be as good as the data you show it, and it never really learns from its own mistakes. When it drifts into a situation the demonstrations didn't cover, it doesn't have a good way to recover, and small errors compound.

What changes with Pi Star 0.6 is that the robot is now actually deployed, it tries the task, and that experience feeds back into training. We use a form of reinforcement learning where the model learns to tell which of its own actions led to better outcomes and which led to worse ones, and then it shifts toward the better ones. On top of that, when a person steps in and corrects the robot mid-task, that correction becomes a very targeted training signal, because it comes exactly in the states where the policy was struggling.

Practically, what you see is a big jump in robustness and throughput. The robot isn't just able to do the task in a demo; it can do it over and over for hours, recover when something goes wrong, and get faster. That's the difference between a cool research video and something you could actually rely on in the real world.

And more broadly, I think it matters because it changes the scaling story. If the only way to improve is more human demonstrations, you're bottlenecked on human time. If robots can improve from their own experience once they're out there working, every deployment becomes a source of data. That's a much more sustainable path, and it's much closer to how people get good at physical skills: you get shown how once, and then you practice.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts imitation of human demonstrations with reinforcement learning from actions the deployed robot takes itself.

r002.rationale: It says robot experience from deployment feeds training and describes repeated deployments as a continuing data source that addresses imitation’s performance ceiling.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest framing is that everything we'd done up to that point, and really everything the field had done with these large vision-language-action models, was fundamentally imitation. You collect a lot of demonstrations, you train the model to reproduce them, and you get something surprisingly general. But there's a ceiling built into that. The policy can only ever be about as good as the data it was shown, and in practice it's usually a bit worse, because the small errors compound. You see it very clearly when you deploy. The robot does something slightly off, lands in a state the demonstrators never visited, and now it has no idea what to do.

So the thing that made Pi Star 0.6 feel different to me is that the robot's own attempts become the training signal. You run the policy, it succeeds sometimes, fails sometimes, you have a way to tell those apart, whether that's a learned value function or human feedback or some mix, and you feed that back in. And the important part is that this is data from exactly the distribution the robot actually operates in. It's not what a human did with a teleop rig. It's what this robot did, with its own errors, its own recovery attempts, in its own environment.

Once you have that loop closing, two things happen. One, the robot gets better at the things it was already doing, so throughput goes up, failure rates go down, and it does this without us collecting more demonstrations. Two, and this is the part I find more exciting, it starts to recover from situations we never explicitly taught it. Because it has seen itself get into trouble and get back out.

And I'd say philosophically this is the thing that has always been the promise of reinforcement learning in robotics. It just never really worked at scale with real hardware before, because the policies were starting from nothing and the exploration was too expensive. What changed is that you now start from a model that already knows how to do the task roughly, from the imitation pretraining, so the robot's experience is actually informative rather than mostly noise. That combination, a strong prior plus learning from its own practice, is what I think of as the significant change. It's the point where the system stops being a replay of human data and starts to be something that improves on its own.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts imitation of human teleoperation demonstrations with learning from the robot’s own policy attempts, including successes and failures, and identifies this as reinforcement learning in practice.

r002.rationale: It describes a continuing loop of collecting and feeding back the robot’s own real-world attempts, and says this lets performance improve beyond the ceiling of demonstration-only training.

astra-6.text:
I think the significant change is that the robot’s own experience becomes a source of improvement. With imitation learning, you collect demonstrations and train the robot to reproduce what a person did. That’s a powerful starting point, but when the robot makes a mistake, the demonstration doesn’t necessarily tell it how to recover or which alternative would have worked better.

Learning from its own experience gives it that feedback. It can attempt a task, see how well it did, and use that outcome to improve its behavior. So you’re moving from learning what actions look like to learning which actions actually lead to success. It doesn’t eliminate the need for human demonstrations, but it opens up a way for the robot to improve beyond simply copying them.

r001.rationale: It contrasts copying human demonstrations with the robot attempting tasks, evaluating outcomes, and improving its own behavior. This conveys the shift to learning from experience gathered through its actions.

r002.rationale: It says own experience can help the robot improve beyond copying, but does not identify an ongoing stream of real-world experience as the input that overcomes a prior performance plateau.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the significant change is that the robot’s experience becomes a source of improvement, rather than us relying entirely on people to demonstrate what it should do. With demonstrations, you teach the robot by showing it successful behavior. But when the robot acts on its own, it encounters situations where its behavior doesn’t quite work, and those are precisely the situations we want it to learn from.

That’s the opportunity with learning from experience: you can use the outcomes of the robot’s attempts to improve its policy. The robot isn’t just trying to reproduce what a person did; it’s learning which actions actually help it complete the task. Human demonstrations are still valuable, but you now have a way to improve beyond imitation by collecting experience with the robot itself.

r001.rationale: It contrasts learning by human demonstrations with learning from the robot’s own attempts, and says those outcomes improve its policy.

r002.rationale: It mentions collecting the robot’s experience but does not identify an ongoing stream of real-world experience as the missing input or connect it to overcoming a performance plateau.
